cards.subject: The chasuble, laid out on a vesting counter, as an illuminated still life, seen from low at three-quarters along the counter: a Roman fiddleback chasuble of stiff deep green silk damask spread flat on the broad top of a pale oak sacristy vesting counter, its back uppermost, a broad straight column of gold embroidery running down its middle from collar to hem; laid across it in the traditional way, ready for vesting, the matching green stole and maniple with their small gold crosses. Behind it, a wall of tall oak drawers. Late-afternoon sunlight slants through tall clear windows in long warm bars across the green silk, catching the gold thread. Ample, calm, enfolding. No figures.
cards.frame: instead of the arched window, a centred gold-edged QUATREFOIL medallion on a deep blue ground scattered with small gold stars, holding a single object like an illuminated still life; no halo, no figures
cards.basis: 'The vestment proper to the Priest Celebrant at Mass ... is the chasuble worn, unless otherwise indicated, over the alb and stole' (GIRM 337); it is prepared for the priest with the alb and stole (GIRM 119). It follows the colour of the day (GIRM 346): the card shows green, the colour of Ordinary Time (346c), because the excerpt is the Entrance Antiphon of a Mass for Various Needs, which is 'celebrated in the color proper to the day or the time of year' (GIRM 347; the formulary's own colour in the data is green), and because green sets it apart from batch 50's violet stole and this batch's rose dalmatic. The GIRM leaves the form to the Conferences (GIRM 342) and wants beauty 'in the material used and in the design' (GIRM 344): the ample cut and the Y-shaped orphrey cross are traditional choices (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Chasuble'). The Encyclopedia calls the chasuble the vestment 'covering all the rest', and gives the words at its bestowal in ordination: 'the priestly vestment, by which is signified charity'; the excerpt, Col 3:14-15, puts on love 'over all things'.

cards.subject: The dalmatic, displayed, as an illuminated still life, seen at eye level a little from the left: a knee-length tunic of stiff rose-coloured silk damask cut in the Roman manner, with short square sleeves and open sides, hangs spread to its full width on a broad wooden cross-bar inside a tall glass-fronted walnut vestment case lined with deep indigo velvet. Two narrow vertical bands of gold embroidery run down from its upper edge to its hem, joined near the hem and below the collar by two narrow gold cross-bands, and a short gold fringe edges each sleeve. A soft light from inside the top of the case falls on the rose silk and glints on the gold; faint reflections in the glass. Joyful, festive, ready to serve. No figures.
cards.frame: instead of the arched window, a centred gold-edged QUATREFOIL medallion on a deep blue ground scattered with small gold stars, holding a single object like an illuminated still life; no halo, no figures
cards.basis: 'The vestment proper to the Deacon is the dalmatic, worn over the alb and stole; however, the dalmatic may be omitted out of necessity or on account of a lesser degree of solemnity' (GIRM 338; also GIRM 119). It follows the colour of the day (GIRM 346): the card shows rose, which 'may be used, where it is the practice, on Gaudete Sunday (Third Sunday of Advent)' (346f), because the excerpt is the First Reading of Gaudete Sunday, Year B, and because rose sets it apart from batch 50's violet stole and this batch's green chasuble. The GIRM gives no form (GIRM 342): the Roman form, knee-length with wide sleeves and two narrow vertical stripes joined near the hem by two narrow cross-stripes, and the fringe on the sleeves, are traditional choices (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Dalmatic'). The Encyclopedia calls the dalmatic 'a festal garment' and gives the words of the bishop at a deacon's ordination: 'May the Lord clothe thee with the garment of salvation and with the vesture of praise', the image of Is 61:10 in the excerpt, whose Latin in the same file is 'induit me vestimentis salutis'.
